title: Superotemporal Retinal Tears: Risk, Laser & Prophylaxis
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to the diagnosis and management of superior retinal breaks. Focused on high-risk features like myopia, lattice degeneration, and trauma, with evidence-based protocols for laser retinopexy to prevent rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Overview
sections.content: A retinal tear is a full-thickness break in the neurosensory retina, typically resulting from vitreoretinal traction during a Posterior Vitreous Detachment (PVD). Superotemporal tears are clinically critical because gravity facilitates the rapid downward spread of subretinal fluid, leading to macula-threatening rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) faster than inferior breaks.

rows: Plug of retina pulled completely free

sections.title: Clinical Presentation: Symptoms
content: Photopsia: Flashing lights in periphery (dynamic traction)
Floaters: Sudden onset 'cobwebs' or 'flies'
Weiss Ring: Circular floater signifying complete PVD
Tobacco Dust: Shafer's sign (RPE cells in vitreous)
Curtain Sign: Progressive visual field loss (indicates RD evolution)

sections.title: The Ocular Examination Protocol
content: 1. Wide Dilation: Phenylephrine 2.5% + Tropicamide 1%.
2. Slit-Lamp Bio: Search for Shafer's sign in anterior vitreous.
3. Indirect Ophthalmoscopy: 20D/28D lens 360-degree sweep.
4. Scleral Depression: Mandatory to visualize the Ora and flap base.
5. Three-Mirror Gonioscopy: Detailed view of suspicious lesions.

sections.title: Shafer's Sign (Tobacco Dust)
content: Presence of pigment cells in the anterior vitreous.
90% predictive value for a retinal break in the setting of acute PVD.
Must perform exhaustive scleral depression to find the break.

rows: Inner wall elevation, no tobacco dust, absolute scotoma
Flat, milky appearance, common in blacks/myopes
Yellow-white atrophic patches, prominent choroidal vessels

sections.title: AAO PPP Indications for Laser
content: Symptomatic Horseshoe Tears: Treat urgently (high risk of RD).
Acute Symptomatic Operculated Tears: Usually safe to observe unless high risk (e.g. fellow eye RD).
Traumatic Dialysis: Treat promptly even if asymptomatic.
Lattice with Symptomatic Tear: Treat the tear and the lattice.
Asymptomatic Lattice: Observation generally recommended, except in high-risk eyes (Aphakia, Fellow eye RD).
Asymptomatic Horseshoe Tears: Controversial; many treat if large or superior.

sections.title: Laser Retinopexy Technique
content: 1. Anesthesia: Topical Proparacaine (Sub-tenon's if scleral depression needed).
2. Wavelength: 532nm (Green) or 810nm (Diode).
3. Spot Size: 200-500 microns (depends on contact lens).
4. Duration: 0.1 to 0.2 seconds.
5. Application: 3 rows of nearly confluent burns (Grade II-III white) surrounding the break.
6. Coverage: Ensure burns extend to the Ora Serrata for U-tears.

content.explanation: Factors making a break high risk: S: Symptoms (acute), A: Aphakia/Pseudophakia, L: Lattice (extensive), T: Trauma or Top (Superior) location.

sections.title: Complications of Laser Prophylaxis
content: Epiretinal Membrane (ERM) formation (~3-5%).
Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) - rare with peripheral laser.
Inadvertent foveal burn (ensure orientation).
Iatrogenic retinal breaks.
Failure: Progression to RD despite laser (usually due to inadequate treatment of the anterior horn).

sections.title: Emergency Signs: Failed Prophylaxis
content: Increasing photopsia/floaters post-laser.
Subretinal fluid extending beyond the laser barricade.
Visual field defect ('Shadow' or 'Curtain').
Decreased visual acuity (Macular involvement).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Fellows
content: Always treat the 'horns' (anterior edges) of a horseshoe tear all the way to the Ora.
In cases of Vitreous Hemorrhage where the retina isn't visible, B-scan is mandatory to rule out RD.
Laser takes 7-14 days to reach maximum chorioretinal adhesion strength.
Advise patients: No heavy lifting or jarring exercise for 2 weeks post-laser.

sections.title: Evidence & Landmark Studies
sections.content: The AAO Preferred Practice Patterns (PPP) and several retrospective series (e.g., Byer et al.) emphasize that while 10% of the population has retinal breaks, only 1 in 10,000 develops RD annually. This underscores the importance of treating only 'high-risk' symptomatic breaks. The PIVOT trial and other surgical studies focus on RD repair, but the consensus remains that laser retinopexy is the gold standard for symptomatic tear prophylaxis with a >95% success rate.
